heading: PROPHET SHUʿAYB (AS)
title: THE MEASURE OF HONESTY
themes: Tawḥīd • Fairness • Trust • Honesty • Courage • Reform • Responsibility
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 8 SELECTED COMPLETE AYĀT
reviewNote: EDITORIAL WORKING EDITION — Arabic, translations, Tafsīr, child safety and scholarly review required before release.
introduction: Volume Twelve continues the ʿIBRAH Junior project after Prophet Ayyūb (AS). This world introduces Prophet Shuʿayb (AS), whom Allah sent to Madyan, through the explicit Qur’anic account. His message joined worship of Allah alone with integrity in measurement, justice in people’s property, and resistance to corruption. The Qur’an also records opposition to his call, his desire for reform, and his reliance upon Allah. The full account is read across al-Aʿrāf 7:85–93, Hūd 11:84–95, al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:176–191 and al-ʿAnkabūt 29:36–37.

As in the previous volumes, the contemporary storyline belongs to Imaan, Akhlaq, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina. Their projects and conversations are fictional educational examples, not events from Shuʿayb’s life. We do not invent biographical information, identify the elderly father in Mūsā’s narrative with Shuʿayb as established fact, or equate school errors with the punishment of a people.

stories.title: The Missing Weight
stories.subtitle: THE EXHIBITION BEGINS WITH A QUESTION OF FAIRNESS

blocks.text: The next learning world began with a very ordinary object: a small scale on Sheikh Uncle’s Academy table. The students were preparing a charity exhibition where families could buy carefully measured packets of dates and dried fruit. Mohsin was in charge of carrying the supplies; Mohsina had made the signs. Imaan checked the names, while Akhlaq proudly supervised the scale. “We have a perfect system,” he announced. Then a younger pupil placed the empty tray on the scale and noticed that the pointer did not begin at zero. “Maybe it is close enough,” Akhlaq said. “A little difference cannot matter.” Imaan was not convinced. She tested it twice, then asked Sir Zameer to inspect the instrument. The pointer was wrongly set. Every packet would have been short of its stated amount. Some classmates wanted to open the stall because parents were already arriving. Sir Zameer suggested they stop and correct the scale first. Akhlaq worried that admitting a mistake would make their team look foolish. “But if we know the measure is wrong,” Imaan asked, “can we honestly sell it as correct?” That evening, Dadi Jaan opened Sūrah Hūd and explained Allah’s message through Shuʿayb (AS): worship Allah alone and do not decrease measure or weight. She reminded the children that this was not merely a lesson in measuring fruit; the Prophet called his people to Tawḥīd and justice, and the Qur’an records their serious resistance. Their school project was only a small application. The children returned the next morning, recalibrated the scale with adult help, and carefully rechecked the packets. Their sign now read: A FAIR MEASURE IS A PROMISE WE CAN KEEP. Akhlaq did not receive a prize for discovering the mistake. He had nearly ignored it. Yet he was relieved that they had chosen to correct it before it harmed anyone.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Fairness begins by noticing and correcting what is wrong.

At the fruit table, Akhlaq and Mohsin prepared two boxes of oranges. Each box was supposed to contain the same amount. Mohsin counted the pieces, while Akhlaq rushed to seal the lids before the queue became long. When the first customers arrived, a younger child pointed at one box. “Why does that one look smaller?” Akhlaq opened it and counted again. The child was right: several oranges had rolled beneath the table. Mohsin said they could replace them later. Imaan said the customer should receive the correct amount now. “What if nobody had noticed?” Akhlaq asked. “Then it would still be unfair,” Mohsina answered. Salamah, who was helping at the exhibition, reminded them that honesty does not begin only when someone is watching. She mentioned the Qur’anic command to give full measure and not deprive people of their belongings. The children decided to inspect every box and explain the delay politely. One impatient visitor complained. Akhlaq felt a flash of irritation, but he replied truthfully that they had found a counting error. The visitor thanked him for correcting it. At the end of the morning, they had sold fewer boxes than planned. But the numbers in their record were accurate, and no buyer received less than promised. On the way home, Akhlaq said, “We did not win the fastest-stall award.” “What matters more?” asked Salaam. Akhlaq thought carefully. “That people received what belonged to them.” Dadi Jaan later added that fair trade is part of an obedient life, not a separate subject outside faith. Their scale now reminded them of something larger than oranges: another person’s right must not shrink because we feel rushed.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Give others their full due, even if speed or popularity suffers.

stories.title: The Borrowed Box
stories.subtitle: PEOPLE HAVE A RIGHT TO WHAT BELONGS TO THEM

blocks.text: The next difficulty had nothing to do with money. A box of coloured paper was missing from the art room, and several students assumed that Mohsina had forgotten to return it. She had borrowed some sheets for the exhibition, but she was certain she had brought the box back. Whispers began while the teacher checked the storeroom. Imaan remembered using a similar box to finish the display cards. After searching her bag, she found it beneath her notebook. “Oh no,” she whispered. She had taken it by mistake. For a moment she considered placing it quietly on the shelf and telling no one. It would be easier. Then she saw how upset Mohsina had become. She went straight to Sir Zameer, explained what happened, and apologised to her friend. He thanked her for returning the materials and for correcting the misunderstanding, but asked her to label shared supplies carefully next time. During their reading session, Sheikh Uncle explained that Sūrah Hūd does not limit fairness to numbers on a scale; it also warns against diminishing what belongs to other people. The children discussed the difference between an honest mistake and a deliberate attempt to keep what was not theirs. Both may need repair, but an honest confession gives others a chance to put things right. Akhlaq suggested they make a borrowing register. Mohsin designed a shelf label, and Mohsina agreed to manage the returns with another pupil so that no single child carried all the blame. By Friday the box was back where it belonged. Imaan discovered that admitting a mistake could feel uncomfortable and still be the best way to protect friendship. She wrote in her diary: RESTORE WHAT IS NOT YOURS; CORRECT WHAT YOU HAVE SAID.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Tell the truth and restore what belongs to others.

stories.title: The Shortcut Through the Gate
stories.subtitle: DO NOT MAKE THE WAY UNSAFE

blocks.text: Rain forced the school to move its community exhibition indoors. Parents and children streamed through a narrow hallway, and a group of older pupils began using the side gate as a shortcut. They laughed whenever a younger child hesitated. One boy stood in the doorway with his arms spread, pretending he was a guard who could decide who entered. Akhlaq thought it was a game until a child carrying books stumbled while trying to squeeze past. Imaan hurried to alert the teacher. Sir Zameer moved the tables, opened a safer route, and asked the pupils to stop blocking the passage. Later he read the warning in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf about threatening people along roads and turning them away from the path of Allah. He explained that the historical warning concerned the wrongdoing of Shuʿayb’s people and their opposition to guidance. The school hallway was not the historical event, and the pupils should not turn the verse into a label for classmates. Instead they could learn a limited practical lesson: do not use strength or position to intimidate others, and make safe access possible. Mohsin noticed that someone using a walking aid would struggle with the old arrangement. The team made more space, added clear direction signs, and asked the staff to supervise the gate. Akhlaq was tempted to confront the boy angrily, but Salaam reminded him that children should not take responsibility for controlling unsafe behaviour alone. They should seek trusted adults. At closing time the hallway was calmer. Their best achievement was not a dramatic confrontation but a clear, welcoming path.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Choose safe access; ask a trusted adult when others threaten or intimidate.

Akhlaq had been appointed queue organiser for the final exhibition rehearsal. He loved the clipboard, the tidy lines and the authority of saying, “Please wait your turn.” For twenty minutes everything worked. Then he saw his friends gathering near the front. He slipped between two students and began talking as though he belonged there. “Excuse me,” said a younger pupil, “you told us nobody should cut the line.” Akhlaq felt his cheeks warm. “I am helping the organisers,” he replied. But he had not been asked to move ahead; he simply wanted to join his friends. Imaan quietly invited him to the back of the queue. He hesitated, then went. In the afternoon, Dadi Jaan helped them read the meaning of Sūrah Hūd 11:88. Shuʿayb (AS) declared that he did not want to do the things he forbade his people; he sought reform to the best of his ability and relied upon Allah. “Was his message only a rule about queues?” Akhlaq asked. “No,” she replied. “It was much greater: divine guidance, worship and justice. But it teaches us that sincerity matters.” The next day Akhlaq helped create a system where organisers took turns serving and waiting. He removed his own name from the first slot to show that the system applied fairly. Nobody forced him to make a public confession; he quietly fixed the problem. The clipboard no longer felt like a crown. It felt like a responsibility. At the bottom he wrote: IF I ASK FOR FAIRNESS, I MUST TRY TO BE FAIR TOO.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Do not demand standards from others while excusing yourself.

A newly printed notice appeared above the exhibition stall: SPECIAL BOX — TWICE THE FRUIT FOR THE SAME PRICE. Mohsin was delighted; it sounded exciting. But when Imaan compared the standard and special boxes, she discovered the contents were equal. A printer had copied the wrong description from a draft sign. The students debated whether to change it. “Customers might like the offer,” one pupil said. “And the money is for charity.” Sir Zameer asked whether a good purpose made a false description acceptable. It did not. The team corrected the sign before any purchase and informed the organisers. Some were embarrassed because the mistake had already been photographed. Mohsina proposed a simple explanation rather than blaming whoever typed it. At home, Salamah discussed how Prophet Shuʿayb (AS) called people to justice in trade and warned against depriving others of their due. She also reminded them that the Qur’an records his words about the good that Allah leaves through lawful conduct. Akhlaq understood that doing something for a worthy cause never gives permission to mislead someone. The corrected sign was less exciting but true. When families asked why it changed, the children said they had noticed an error and repaired it. Their exhibition still raised money for books, and the buyers knew exactly what they were receiving. Imaan's new rule was simple: BE PRECISE WHEN PEOPLE DEPEND ON YOUR WORDS.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Good causes never justify misleading descriptions.

Two boys from another class disliked the fairness notices. They said the exhibition would be more profitable if students stopped checking everything. When Akhlaq objected, one boy laughed. “Have you become the honesty police?” The group around him laughed too. Akhlaq wanted to shout back, but Imaan gently stopped him. They told Sir Zameer about the comments. He listened, checked that no one was being threatened, and reminded the children that disagreement can be handled without humiliation. Later he explained how the Qur’an describes serious resistance faced by Shuʿayb (AS), including mockery and threats. His mission was revelation; the classroom disagreement was a modern situation with much lower stakes. Still, they could learn not to abandon what was right merely for applause. Sir Zameer invited the two groups to inspect the exhibition records together with an adult present. Once they understood the process, they agreed that accurate measures protected buyers and the reputation of the project. The boys were not made villains in the final presentation; they were given the opportunity to improve their idea. Imaan told Akhlaq, “Courage does not always sound loud.” He nodded. Sometimes it sounded like a calm explanation, a truthful correction, or a request for help from the right adult.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Hold to what is right without humiliation or unsafe confrontation.

At last the exhibition opened. Visitors walked past the reading corner, the labelled shelves, the charity stall, and a banner that said HONESTY IS MORE THAN A NUMBER. The children had worked hard, but Dadi Jaan still asked one final question. “What did Prophet Shuʿayb (AS) teach his people before he spoke about weighing and measuring?” Akhlaq knew. “To worship Allah alone.” “And what did he say about his own effort?” Imaan replied, “He wanted reform as much as he could, and success is from Allah.” Sheikh Uncle displayed the relevant Qur’anic references and explained that the historical accounts include rejection and divine judgment. Those events should be learned with respect and never turned into a frightening guessing game. After the guests left, Mohsin proposed a scoring board for children who had been ‘most honest’ during the week. Salamah declined. “We may celebrate careful work,” she said, “but we cannot measure a child’s faith or private sincerity.” Instead, each pupil chose one action to carry forward. Imaan would return borrowed things promptly. Mohsina would correct mistaken descriptions kindly. Mohsin would check quantities. Akhlaq would practise the rules he asked others to follow. Dadi Jaan wrote their choices on blank paper leaves and added them to the family’s growing learning tree. The compass stayed closed in its case. This time the direction did not need to glow. It was already written clearly in what they hoped to do: WORSHIP ALLAH, TELL THE TRUTH, AND GIVE PEOPLE THEIR DUE.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Faithful character is practised, not publicly scored.

synthesis.text: The revealed account and its limits

Allah sent Shuʿayb (AS) to Madyan and called the people through him to worship Allah alone. The verses condemn short measure, injustice in others’ property, corruption, and obstruction of the path of guidance. Shuʿayb declared that he did not seek to practise what he forbade, that he wanted reform within his ability, and that his success and reliance were upon Allah. The Qur’an records rejection and divine judgment; those historical events must be presented with respect, without invented dialogue or child-facing simulations of destruction. This volume does not identify an unnamed elder from other Qur’anic narratives as Shuʿayb with certainty.
Seven lasting lessons
Worship Allah alone and remember Him in daily choices.
Give people the full and accurate measure promised to them.
Do not take away what belongs to another person or damage their reputation with guesses.
Keep community spaces safe and seek an adult’s help when someone intimidates or threatens.
Follow the standards you recommend to others.
Correct errors and seek Allah’s forgiveness without despair or shame.
Work for useful reform, thank contributors, and rely on Allah rather than applause.

Final achievement design

An episode or mission can unlock a source verse, vocabulary cards and the next learning world. Engagement-based progression must not imply that a learner is more holy or more like a Prophet. Review of sources and compassionate feedback matter more than speed.
